Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D levels were not associated with depressive symptoms in Korean female nurses.
Sentence: "Vitamin D levels were not associated with body mass index, physical activity, and depressive symptoms."
Measured as: depressive symptoms
Population: 1594 registered Korean female nurses aged 20 to 45 years
Intervention: Serum 25(OH)D level (observational, not assigned)
Comparator: Higher vs lower vitamin D levels across participants
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 1,594
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

## Study B
Found: benefit
Claim: Winter light therapy reduced depression scores in adolescents.
Sentence: "Winter light therapy increases vitamin D (Δ = 8.2 ng/mL, p < 0.001) and reduces depression (ΔPHQ-9=-3.1, p = 0.005)."
Measured as: depression (PHQ-9)
Population: Chinese adolescents in winter RCTs (N = 200)
Intervention: Winter light therapy
Comparator: Not reported
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 7,321
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

content.text: {"rationale":"Study B's exposure is light therapy, which raises vitamin D only as a side effect, so it is not a vitamin D comparison.","verdict":"off_question","reason":null,"also_differs":[],"detail":"exposure: winter light therapy (not vitamin D supplementation or level)"}
